items.signText:
Tom – the printer on our floor has broken down again and the engineer can't come until Thursday. Until then, please use the one on the second floor, but remember it only prints in black and white.
Priya
items.question: Why has Priya written to Tom?
options: a) To warn him that colour printing is no longer possible in the office
b) To tell him where he can print until the printer is repaired
c) To ask him to contact the engineer before Thursday
items.explanation: Priya writes 'Until then, please use the one on the second floor', so she is telling Tom which printer to use until the engineer comes. She does not ask him to contact the engineer, and she only says the second-floor printer is black and white, not that colour printing is impossible for good.

items.signText:
Jack – Mr Evans from Greenfield Ltd phoned at 10.30. He can't come to this afternoon's meeting and would like to move it to tomorrow at the same time. Could you call him back to confirm?
Sam
items.question: What does Jack need to do?
options: a) Phone Mr Evans to confirm the new meeting time
b) Tell Mr Evans that the meeting will start later this afternoon
c) Wait for Mr Evans to phone again later today
items.explanation: Sam writes 'Could you call him back to confirm?' after explaining that Mr Evans wants to move the meeting to tomorrow at the same time. So Jack must phone Mr Evans; he is not asked to wait for another call, and the meeting is moving to tomorrow, not starting later today.

items.signText:
To: All staff
From: Maria (IT)
The office Wi-Fi password is changing on Monday. Everyone will receive the new password by text message early on Monday morning. Please don't ask reception for it, as they won't have it.
items.question: How will staff get the new Wi-Fi password?
options: a) They will be sent it in a text message.
b) They can collect it from reception on Monday.
c) They have to choose a new one before Monday.
items.explanation: Maria writes 'Everyone will receive the new password by text message early on Monday morning'. She says reception 'won't have it', and staff do not choose the password themselves.

items.signText:
MEETING ROOM 3
This room is booked for the sales team every Tuesday from 9 to 11 a.m. If you need it at any other time, please write your name and the time on the list at reception, not on this door.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The sales team must write their names on the door of the room.
b) Anyone can use this room on Tuesday mornings if it is empty.
c) People who want the room at other times should book it at reception.
items.explanation: The notice says 'If you need it at any other time, please write your name and the time on the list at reception'. The room is booked for the sales team on Tuesday mornings, so it is not free for anyone then, and names should go on the reception list, 'not on this door'.

items.signText:
STAFF KITCHEN
The fridge will be cleaned on Friday at 4 p.m. Any food or drink without a name on it will be thrown away, but items with a name label can stay.
items.question: What should staff do?
options: a) Stay out of the kitchen while the fridge is being cleaned.
b) Clean the fridge themselves on Friday at 4 p.m.
c) Put a name label on any food they want to keep.
items.explanation: The notice says food 'without a name on it will be thrown away' and 'items with a name label can stay', so staff should label food they want to keep. The kitchen is not closed, and the notice says the fridge 'will be cleaned', not that staff must clean it.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.textTitle: The teenager who helped a whole street
lesenParts.text:
When sixteen-year-old Maya Collins started building an app in her bedroom two years ago, she had no idea that it would soon be used by more than fifty thousand people. 'Honestly, I just wanted to solve a problem in my own family,' she says.

The problem began one winter. Maya's grandmother slipped on some ice and broke her leg. She lived alone, and although Maya's parents visited as often as they could, they both worked long hours in another town. 'Gran's neighbours kept telling us they would happily help her with shopping or collecting medicine,' Maya explains. 'But they never knew when she actually needed something, and she was too proud to knock on their doors and ask.'

That gave Maya the idea for Next Door, an app which lets older people post small requests that neighbours nearby can accept with one click. There was only one difficulty: Maya had never written a line of computer code. She spent the next six months teaching herself from free online videos, often working until midnight at weekends. 'My first version was a disaster,' she laughs. 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once.'

Help came from an unexpected place. Maya's computer science teacher, Mr Okafor, noticed her working on the app during a lunch break and offered to look at it with her. 'He didn't fix it for me,' she says. 'He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong. That was much more useful.'

After a few more months of testing with her grandmother's neighbours, Maya put Next Door online. At first only a handful of families in her street joined, but then a local radio station interviewed her, and the number of users grew almost overnight. Today the app is used in towns all over the country.

Several companies have since offered to buy Next Door, but Maya has turned them all down. 'They wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it,' she says. 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money, so that's not going to happen.'

Maya admits it hasn't always been easy to balance the app with her schoolwork, especially during exams. She now spends only Sunday afternoons on it, and a small team of volunteers answers users' messages during the week.

Her advice for other young people with an idea is simple. 'Don't wait until you feel ready, because you never will. Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.'

questions.question: Why did Maya decide to create the app?
questions.explanation: Maya says the neighbours 'would happily help' but 'they never knew when she actually needed something'. Her grandmother did not ask for help at all – she was 'too proud to knock on their doors and ask' – so the neighbours never refused her.
options: a) Her grandmother had asked the neighbours for help and they had refused.
b) She wanted to enter a competition for young app designers.
c) Her parents asked her to find a way of looking after her grandmother.
d) Her grandmother's neighbours wanted to help but did not know when.

questions.question: What does Maya say about the first version of Next Door?
questions.explanation: Maya says 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once'. She spent six months teaching herself, not a few weeks, and her teacher only helped her later, after he noticed her working on the app at lunch.
options: a) It stopped working as soon as a few people used it together.
b) It took her only a few weeks to build from online videos.
c) She built it with help from her teacher.
d) Her parents helped her to test it at weekends.

questions.question: How did Mr Okafor help Maya?
questions.explanation: Maya says 'He didn't fix it for me. He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong.' She found the online videos herself, and he saw her working on the app during a lunch break, not in lessons.
options: a) He recommended some free online videos to her.
b) He let her work on the app during his lessons.
c) He asked her questions until she saw her own mistakes.
d) He corrected the problems in her code himself at lunch.

questions.question: Why has Maya refused to sell the app?
questions.explanation: The companies 'wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it', and Maya says 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money'. She does not mention the amount of money offered, and she does not want anyone to pay.
options: a) The companies did not offer her enough money.
b) She wants it to stay free for people who might not be able to pay.
c) She is worried that selling it would take up too much of her time.
d) She is planning to charge users for it herself.

questions.question: What advice does Maya give to young people with an idea?
questions.explanation: Maya says 'Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.' She also says 'Don't wait until you feel ready', which is the opposite of waiting until you have all the skills, and she sees mistakes as the way to learn rather than something to avoid.
options: a) Ask an expert to check your idea before you do anything.
b) Try hard to avoid making mistakes in the early stages.
c) Start small and accept that things will go wrong.
d) Wait until you have all the skills you need before starting.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Last June, my sister Clare and I decided to spend a week cycling along the coast of Cornwall, from Padstow to Penzance. Neither of us had any experience of cycling holidays, and we weren't particularly fit either. (1) ______ We simply thought it would be a cheap and healthy way to see a beautiful part of the country.

We hired our bikes from a small shop in Padstow. The owner, a friendly man called Pete, spent almost an hour checking that our seats were the right height and showing us how to fix a flat tyre. (2) ______ He also gave us a map with the quietest roads marked in red, which turned out to be extremely useful.

The first day was hard work. The coast road goes up and down constantly, and by lunchtime our legs were aching. (3) ______ Luckily, the views of the sea from the top of each hill made all the effort worthwhile, and by the evening we were already feeling stronger.

On the third morning, just outside the village of St Agnes, Clare's back tyre suddenly went flat. There was no bike shop for miles and hardly any traffic on the road. (4) ______ Twenty minutes later we were back on our bikes, feeling rather proud of ourselves.

Each night we stayed in a small guest house, which we had booked before we left home. (5) ______ Most of them were also happy to let us keep our bikes in their garden or garage overnight, and one even washed our muddy clothes for us.

By the time we reached Penzance, we had cycled nearly two hundred kilometres. We were tired, sunburnt and very happy, and we are already planning next year's trip.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: The writer has just said they had no experience and 'weren't particularly fit'; 'In fact' explains that they did not choose the trip because they loved cycling, and the next sentence gives the real reason: 'We simply thought it would be a cheap and healthy way to see a beautiful part of the country'. The sentence about Clare having cycled the route before cannot fit, because the text says 'Neither of us had any experience'.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
questions.explanation: 'This' refers to Pete showing them 'how to fix a flat tyre', and 'we were glad of it later' prepares for the flat tyre on the third morning. The sentence about repairing the tyre cannot go here, because nothing has broken yet.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
questions.explanation: The road 'goes up and down constantly' and their legs were aching, so they had to push their bikes up 'the steepest hills'. The next sentence continues the idea: 'the views of the sea from the top of each hill made all the effort worthwhile'. Taking the train cannot fit, as they cycled all the way to Penzance.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
questions.explanation: There was 'no bike shop for miles', but 'however' shows a contrast: because Pete had taught them, they could 'repair it' (the flat tyre) themselves, and 'Twenty minutes later we were back on our bikes'. Camping in a field cannot fit, because they continued cycling and stayed in guest houses.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
questions.explanation: 'The owners' are the owners of the guest houses mentioned just before, and the next sentence, 'Most of them were also happy to let us keep our bikes…', continues describing them. Camping in a field contradicts the guest houses they had booked.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Most of us know we should eat more fruit and vegetables, but changing the way we eat is not always easy. Experts say the secret is to (1) ______ small changes, one at a time, rather than trying to change everything at once.

For example, instead of (2) ______ breakfast because you are in a hurry, try preparing something the night before. A bowl of porridge with some fresh fruit will (3) ______ you full of energy until lunchtime, and you will be less likely to buy biscuits or crisps during the morning.

It is also a good idea to (4) ______ attention to how much sugar there is in the food you buy. Many products which are (5) ______ as healthy, such as fruit yoghurts and cereal bars, actually contain a surprising amount of it. Reading the labels carefully in the supermarket only takes a few minutes.

Finally, try not to eat your meals in front of the television or your phone. When your mind is on something else, it is easy to eat far more than you need without (6) ______ it.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'make changes' ('the secret is to make small changes'). We do not say 'do changes', 'take changes' or 'get changes' in English.
options: a) get
b) do
c) take
d) make

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: To 'skip breakfast' means not to eat it, which matches 'because you are in a hurry'. 'Passing', 'dropping' and 'jumping' are not used with a meal to mean not eating it.
options: a) skipping
b) passing
c) dropping
d) jumping

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'keep somebody + adjective': porridge 'will keep you full of energy'. 'Stay' and 'remain' cannot take an object ('you'), and 'hold you full of energy' is not possible.
options: a) remain
b) keep
c) stay
d) hold

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'pay attention to' something: 'pay attention to how much sugar there is'. 'Make', 'put' and 'take' do not go with 'attention' in this way.
options: a) make
b) pay
c) put
d) take

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: Products are 'advertised as healthy' when companies sell them with this message, which contrasts with 'actually contain a surprising amount' of sugar. We cannot say a product is 'informed', 'announced' or 'noticed as healthy'.
options: a) advertised
b) informed
c) announced
d) noticed

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: 'Without noticing it' means without realising what is happening: when your mind is on something else, you eat too much and don't notice. 'Looking it' and 'caring it' are not grammatical (we say 'look at' and 'care about'), and 'paying it' makes no sense here.
options: a) caring
b) paying
c) noticing
d) looking

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text:
Last Saturday, more than eighty volunteers took part (1) ______ our town's first beach clean-up day at Sandy Bay. The idea came from a group of students at the local college, who had become worried about the amount of rubbish on the shore.

Everyone got gloves and a bag and was given one section of the beach to clean, from the car park to the rocks at the far end. You wouldn't expect to find a fridge on a beach, (2) ______ you? Well, we found two! Most of the rubbish, however, was plastic. We counted how (3) ______ bottles we collected: over six hundred. By lunchtime there was (4) ______ much rubbish for one lorry, and the council had to send a second one.

'I found (5) ______ hard to believe how dirty the beach was,' said Jess Taylor, one of the organisers. 'But people who had never met were chatting and laughing together all day.'

The students now hope to hold a clean-up every spring, (6) ______ or not the council helps them again.

questions.question: Gap (1): More than eighty volunteers took part ____ our town's first beach clean-up day.
questions.explanation: 'Take part in something' is a fixed expression meaning 'join an activity'. 'Part' is always followed by 'in' before the event.

questions.question: Gap (2): You wouldn't expect to find a fridge on a beach, ____ you?
questions.explanation: This is a question tag. The main sentence uses 'wouldn't', so the positive tag repeats the same modal: 'would you?'. 'Do you' or 'will you' do not match 'wouldn't'.

questions.question: Gap (3): We counted how ____ bottles we collected: over six hundred.
questions.explanation: 'Bottles' is a plural countable noun, so we ask about quantity with 'how many'. 'How much' is used with uncountable nouns, and 'how few' does not fit 'over six hundred'.

questions.question: Gap (4): The council had to send a second one to take it all ____.
questions.explanation: 'Too much ... for' means more than something can hold: the rubbish did not fit in one lorry, so the council had to send a second one.

questions.question: Gap (5): I found ____ hard to believe how dirty the beach was.
questions.explanation: In 'find + it + adjective + to-infinitive', 'it' is an empty object that stands for the idea that follows ('to believe how dirty the beach was'). Without 'it' the sentence is not correct.

questions.question: Gap (6): The students now hope to hold a clean-up every spring, ____ or not the council helps them again.
questions.explanation: 'Whether or not' means 'it does not matter if'. The students will do it in any case. 'If' is not possible directly before 'or not'.

horenParts.transcript:
Woman: Have you found your phone yet?
Man: Yes, finally. I was sure I'd left it at the gym, so I rang them, but nobody had handed it in.
Woman: Did you look in the kitchen? That's where you usually put it.
Man: I did, twice. In the end it was under the passenger seat in the car. It must have fallen out of my pocket when I drove home.

Dad: What are you having, Ben? The pizza looks good.
Ben: I had pizza last night at Leo's house. I was going to have a salad, but it says here it comes with fish, and I don't like fish.
Dad: The pasta with tomato sauce, then?
Ben: Yes, that's what I'll have.

Man: Are you still going swimming on Tuesdays, Amy?
Amy: No, I gave that up last month. The pool's too far away. I've joined the tennis club near school instead. I've only had two lessons so far, but I love it.
Man: Your brother plays basketball, doesn't he?
Amy: Yes, but that's not for me. I'm too short!

Mum: Have you decided what to get Josh for his birthday?
Girl: Well, I was going to get him a book about football, but he's got loads of those already.
Mum: What about a new football shirt?
Girl: Dad's already bought him one. So I've gone for that new board game he keeps talking about, the one with the space cards. I'll pick it up from the shop on Saturday.

Man: Hi Sara, it's Tom. About the film tonight. The website said it starts at quarter to seven, but I've just phoned the cinema and they've changed it. It's half past seven now, because of some technical problem. So let's still meet at quarter past six for something to eat first. Then we'll have plenty of time. See you later!

Woman: Hello, this is Karen from the community centre, calling about the yoga class on Thursday. You won't need trainers, because we do everything in bare feet. We provide the mats, but please bring your own towel, as we don't have enough for everyone. And don't worry about a notebook. I'll email you the exercises afterwards.

Woman: My bike's got a flat tyre, so I can't cycle in tomorrow.
Man: Will you get the bus, then?
Woman: I thought about it, but there are roadworks on the main road and the buses are taking ages. It's only forty minutes if I walk, and the weather's supposed to be lovely, so I'll just do that.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: If we drive to Edinburgh, we can stop wherever we like on the way.
Man: True, but it's eight hours at the wheel, and parking in the city centre is a nightmare.
Woman: Mm, fair point. And on the train we could read or sleep.
Man: Exactly. And it's not much more expensive if we book now.
Woman: Right, let's do that. But I'm not getting up at five to catch the first one!
Man: No, the one at ten is fine. What about the hotel?
Woman: I'd still prefer somewhere outside the centre. It's quieter.
Man: Hmm. We can sort that out later.

Man: So how was the camping trip? You weren't very keen before you went.
Woman: I know! I thought I'd hate sleeping in a tent, and when it rained on the first night I nearly came home. But honestly, it turned out to be one of the best holidays I've ever had. The campsite was lovely, it cost almost nothing, and I didn't miss my phone at all.
Man: So you'd go again?
Woman: Definitely.

Man: Good morning, Skyway Airlines. Is this about the delays on today's flights?
Woman: No, no, my flight isn't until next week. I'm booked to Rome on the fourteenth, reference AB172. My sister's wedding has been moved, so I won't need to be there until the sixteenth. Could you put me on a flight that day instead? I'm happy to pay the difference. Oh, and I've already read the information about hand luggage, so I don't need to ask about that.
Man: Let me see what I can do.

Man: You're off to Spain again? Visiting your cousins?
Woman: Not this time. They're coming over here in the summer. I've booked a two-week course in Seville. My Spanish is getting really rusty, and I'll need it for my new job.
Man: Lucky you. Seville's near the coast, isn't it?
Woman: Not that near, and anyway I doubt I'll have time for the beach. There are classes every morning and homework every evening!

Woman: How was the hotel in Lisbon?
Man: The rooms were a bit small, and I'd read online that the street outside was noisy, but actually we didn't hear a thing at night. What I really liked was that it was right in the old town, so we could walk everywhere. The breakfast was great too, lots of fresh fruit and local cakes.
Woman: Sounds perfect.

Woman: I'm thinking of doing a weekend in Paris. Have you ever done a city break?
Man: A couple. They're not as expensive as people think, if you book early. And I don't mind all the walking, actually. My problem is that by the time you've found your way around, it's time to go home. I'd rather go somewhere for a whole week and really get to know the place.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Mrs Hughes: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Mrs Hughes, and I'm going to give you the main details of next term's school trip to Barcelona. We'll be away for five days, from the second to the sixth of April. We'll be flying from Manchester, not Liverpool as I said in my first letter, so please remember that.

In Barcelona we'll be staying in a youth hostel near the beach. Students will share rooms of four, and each room has its own bathroom. Breakfast and dinner are included, but you'll have to buy your own lunch, so bring some extra money for that.

On the first full day we'll visit the famous church, the Sagrada Família, and in the afternoon there's a guided walk around the old part of the city. On the Thursday we're going to spend the morning at a local secondary school, where you'll have lessons with Spanish students of your own age. Several of you asked about the football stadium. Unfortunately, it's closed for building work while we're there, so instead we'll go to the science museum, which I promise is great fun.

The total cost of the trip is three hundred and ninety pounds. You need to pay a deposit of eighty pounds by the end of this month, and the rest before the fifteenth of February.

As for what to pack, the weather in April can be quite changeable, so bring a waterproof jacket as well as sun cream. And please don't forget your passport. Every year somebody leaves it at home! Mobile phones are allowed, but you must hand them in to a teacher at ten o'clock each night.

If you have any questions, please email me rather than phoning the school office. Thank you.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Hannah Price, who at just twenty-four is head chef at her own restaurant. Hannah, how did it all start?
Hannah: I was sixteen and I got a Saturday job washing up in a hotel kitchen. I'd always loved cooking at home, so I thought I knew what to expect, but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet… I honestly wasn't sure I'd last. Funnily enough, I didn't mind the washing-up itself. It was nice just to be able to watch the chefs.
Interviewer: And then you went to catering college.
Hannah: That's right. People assume college taught me to cook, but honestly I learnt most of my skills in real kitchens. The written work was easy for me, actually, because I've always liked reading about food. What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business. One of them introduced me to the chef who gave me my first proper job.
Interviewer: Lots of young people get interested in cooking through TV competitions. What do you think of them?
Hannah: My mum loves them, and she's always telling me to apply for one, but I'd never do it, and I don't really watch them myself. My problem is that they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes. Real restaurant work is mostly cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night.
Interviewer: Two years ago you opened your own restaurant. Why?
Hannah: Everyone thinks it's about the money, but I earn less now than when I worked for someone else! And my last boss was brilliant. I still ring him for advice. The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up. It's the kind of food nobody in the city was serving.
Interviewer: What's it like being such a young head chef?
Hannah: Inside my kitchen, it's fine. My team know what I can do. But suppliers sometimes ask to speak to 'the chef' when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me. I don't think being young makes me better or worse at cooking, and I've spent eight years in kitchens, so experience isn't really the issue.
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who want to become chefs?
Hannah: Don't sign up for a course straight away. Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first, even if it's just washing up, and see if you can cope with it. Plenty of people discover it isn't for them, and that's fine. And don't try to learn every kind of food. Getting a few dishes really right is worth much more.

questions.question: How did Hannah feel when she first worked in a kitchen?
questions.explanation: She thought she knew what to expect, 'but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet'. She 'wasn't sure I'd last', so she was not sure about the job, and she says she 'didn't mind the washing-up itself', so she was not bored.
options: a) Surprised by how hard the work was
b) Bored by the simple tasks she had to do
c) Sure that she had chosen the right job

questions.question: What does Hannah say was most useful about catering college?
questions.explanation: She says 'What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business', and one of them introduced her to the chef who gave her her first job. She learnt most of her skills 'in real kitchens', not at college, and the written work was already easy for her.
options: a) She learnt most of her cooking skills there.
b) It helped her with the written work.
c) She met people who helped her find work.

questions.question: What is Hannah's opinion of cooking competitions on TV?
questions.explanation: She says 'they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes', while real work is 'cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night'. She says 'I'd never do it', and it is her mum who loves them; she doesn't really watch them herself.
options: a) She would like to take part in one, as her mum suggests.
b) They are fun to watch with her family.
c) They give the wrong idea of what chefs do.

questions.question: Why did Hannah open her own restaurant?
questions.explanation: 'The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up.' She earns less now than before, and she says her last boss 'was brilliant'.
options: a) She wanted to use food from her local area.
b) She hoped to earn more money than before.
c) She did not get on with her last boss very well.

questions.question: How does Hannah feel about being a young head chef?
questions.explanation: Suppliers 'ask to speak to the chef when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me'. She says being young doesn't make her 'better or worse at cooking', and with eight years in kitchens 'experience isn't really the issue'.
options: a) Worried that she does not have enough experience.
b) Annoyed that some people don't see her as the chef.
c) Sure that her age makes her a better cook.

questions.question: What advice does Hannah give to young people who want to be chefs?
questions.explanation: She says 'Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first … and see if you can cope with it'. She tells them not to sign up for a course straight away, and not to try to learn every kind of food.
options: a) Go to catering college as soon as possible.
b) Get some experience in a real kitchen first.
c) Learn to cook as many kinds of food as possible.

schreibenParts.task:
You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English-speaking friend, Alex, and the notes you have made.

From: Alex
Subject: Guess what!

Hi!

I've got some great news: I've found a flat to rent, and it's in your neighbourhood! I'm moving in at the end of next month. (Note 1: Great!)

I don't know the area at all yet. What's the best thing about living there? (Note 2: Tell Alex)

I'll need to do a lot of shopping for the flat. Where do you think I should go? (Note 3: Suggest…)

And would you like to help me on moving day? I'll buy you lunch! (Note 4: Yes, but…)

See you soon,
Alex

Write your email to Alex using all the notes.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question A: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
My ideal home
Where would your ideal home be? What would it look like, and what would you have in it? Why would it be perfect for you?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question B: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
The old house at the end of the street was finally sold.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Answer the examiner's questions about yourself. Give full answers, with reasons or examples.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. What do you usually have for breakfast?
3. Who does most of the cooking in your home?
4. What's your favourite meal of the day? Why?
5. Tell us about a meal you really enjoyed recently.
6. Do you prefer eating at home or eating out? Why?

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation: Look at the photograph. It shows a family sharing a meal together at home. Tell us what you can see in the photograph. Talk about the people, the food, the place and what you think is happening. You have about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Talk together with your partner. Your class wants to have a meal together to celebrate the end of the school year. Here are some ideas for the meal:

a barbecue in the park
a meal at a pizza restaurant
everyone cooks a dish at home and brings it to school
a picnic on the beach
cooking a meal together in the school kitchen

Talk together about the different ideas and say which would be most enjoyable for the class. Then decide which idea is best.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Discuss these questions with your partner and the examiner:

1. Do you enjoy cooking? What can you cook?
2. Do you think young people should learn to cook at school? Why or why not?
3. What kinds of restaurants are popular in your town?
4. Is it better to eat with your family or with friends? Why?
5. Do people eat more fast food now than in the past? Why do you think this is?
